changes.before: Make notice paragraphs green, ordinary paragraphs maroon, and the footer navy without adding !important.
changes.after: Work out which color wins when two rules choose the same part.

before: A CSS rule affects only elements its selector matches.
When matching rules set the same property, the cascade chooses a winner. Here we compare ordinary stylesheet rules in the same layer, without inline styles or !important.
In the practice, the footer has no color rule of its own, so it can inherit the body color. Give notice paragraphs their own class rule instead of changing every paragraph.
after: A CSS rule can change only the parts that match its selector. A rule for `.notice` does not change every paragraph. It changes only parts with the `notice` class.

The cascade is the set of rules CSS uses to choose a winning setting. This lesson compares normal rules in the same stylesheet layer. A layer is a named group of rules; later lessons explain it. We are not using styles written inside HTML tags or `!important`.
Give the body navy text so the footer can inherit it. Give paragraphs maroon text. Give `.notice` paragraphs green text. Use those selectors to get the result without adding `!important`.

before: Make notice paragraphs green, ordinary paragraphs maroon, and the footer navy without adding !important.
Run the checks and inspect the result.
Change one input or rule and explain what changes.
after: Set the body color to navy and the paragraph color to maroon.
Set `.notice` to green. Leave the footer without its own color rule.

before: .notice matches the two notice paragraphs, not every paragraph.
A later p rule is less specific than .notice.
The footer can inherit body color if you leave it without its own color declaration.
after: `.notice` chooses only parts with the notice class.
The `.notice` rule beats a `p` rule in this example.
Leave the footer’s color unset so it can inherit navy.

before.question: A paragraph has class="tip". The stylesheet first says .tip { color: blue; } and later p { color: red; }. What happens if you move the p rule above the .tip rule?
choices: The paragraph changes from red to blue
The paragraph inherits its parent’s color
before.explanation: The class selector wins over the element selector in either order here. Source order breaks a tie; these selectors do not have equal specificity.

after.question: A paragraph has class="tip". The .tip rule makes it blue, and a later p rule says red. What if you move the p rule above .tip?
choices: It changes from red to blue.
after.explanation: The class rule beats the tag rule in either order here. Order breaks a tie only after the stronger rules have been checked.
